text: Snapchat is an American multimedia social media and instant messaging app developed by Snap Inc., originally known as Snapchat Inc. A core feature of the app is that messages, called "Snaps," are typically accessible for a short time before they expire. The app has evolved from a focus on person-to-person photo sharing to include "Stories" of 24-hour chronological content and "Discover," which allows brands to showcase ad-supported short-form content. Users can store photos in a password-protected area called "My Eyes Only," and the app has reportedly implemented limited end-to-end encryption with plans to expand its use. Snapchat was created by Evan Spiegel, Bobby Murphy, and Reggie Brown, former Stanford University students. Brown introduced the idea of disappearing pictures to Spiegel, who had prior business experience, and the trio brought in Murphy, who had coding experience. They launched the app as "Picaboo" on iOS on July 8, 2011, and later relaunched it as Snapchat in September 2011, focusing on usability and technical improvements. The team retained a mascot named "Ghostface Chillah," inspired by Ghostface Killah of Wu-Tang Clan, designed by Brown. In May 2012, Brown sent an email to Spiegel offering to renegotiate his ownership stake, which lawyers for Snapchat claimed was not valuable, and Brown settled with Spiegel and Murphy for $157.5 million in September 2014, being credited as one of the original authors. In their first blog post on May 9, 2012, CEO Spiegel described Snapchat’s mission as communicating full human emotions, not just idealized images, and positioned it as a solution to the stress caused by permanent online content. As of May 2012, 25 Snapchat images were sent per second, and by November 2012, over one billion photos had been shared, with 20 million per day. Spiegel cited scalability issues as a reason for delivery problems in real-time snaps. The app was released for Android on October 29, 2012. In June 2013, version 5.0 ("Banquo") introduced swipe navigation, double-tap replies, improved friend finder, and in-app profiles, referencing Shakespeare’s Macbeth. Snapkidz, for users under 13, was introduced at the same time, allowing drawing and saving snaps locally but not sending them. By May 2015, users were viewing 2 billion videos per day, reaching 6 billion by November, and 10 billion by 2016. In May 2016, Snapchat raised $1.81 billion in equity, and had nearly 10 million daily active users in the UK by May 31, 2016. In 2016, Investel Capital Corp. sued Snapchat for geofiltering patent infringement, seeking monetary compensation and a ban on future infringement. In September 2016, Snapchat Inc. was renamed Snap Inc. to coincide with the launch of Spectacles, smartglasses that record 10-second videos. Spectacles became available for purchase on February 20, 2017. In February 2017, Snapchat had 160 million daily active users, growing to 166 million by May. In November 2017, a controversial redesign was introduced, making sending snaps and rewatching stories more complicated, combining stories and incoming snaps on one page, and adding featured and sponsored content to Discover. A tweet by Kylie Jenner in February 2018 criticizing the redesign reportedly caused Snap Inc. to lose over $1.3 billion in market value, and over 1.2 million people signed a Change.org petition to remove the update. In December 2019, App Annie named Snapchat the fifth most downloaded mobile app of the decade, based on iOS downloads from 2010 and Android from 2012. In January 2020, Snapchat acquired AI Factory to enhance video capabilities. In November 2020, Snapchat launched Snapchat Spotlight, offering $1 million per day to users who posted viral videos, with no stated criteria or payout distribution; in 2021, the payout model shifted to "millions per month," and as of 2024, the program continued. In June 2022, Snapchat announced Snapchat Plus, a paid subscription offering early access to features, icon changes, and the ability to see which users rewatch stories. By July 2022, the company reported 347 million daily active users, an 18% increase from the prior year, and by August, Snapchat Plus had over 1 million subscribers with four new features added: priority replies, post-view emoji, new Bitmoji content, and new app icons. Snaps can be photos or short videos, edited with filters, effects, text, and drawings, sent privately or to public or semi-public "Stories" or "Our Story." Video snaps were added as a feature option in December 2012, with up to ten-second recordings, later extended to 60 seconds in 10-second intervals. After one viewing, videos disappear by default. Video chat was added on May 1, 2014, along with ephemeral text messaging. Snaps can be viewed for a user-specified time (1 to 10 seconds), with the requirement to hold the screen removed in July 2015; Snapchat does not prevent screenshots but can notify senders if saved, though these can be bypassed. One snap per day can be replayed for free, with the option to purchase extra replays introduced in September 2015 and removed in April 2016. Friends can be added via usernames, phone contacts, Snapcodes, or the "Add Nearby" function. In November 2014, "Snapcash" was introduced, allowing users to send and receive money via private messaging, powered by Square. In July 2016, "Memories" was introduced, allowing users to save snaps and story posts in a private area, edit, and republish them, with timestamps when shared in stories. Content can be searched by date or using local object recognition, and can be stored in "My Eyes Only" with a PIN. In May 2017, unlimited viewing time was introduced, with content disappearing after deliberate closure. New tools included drawing with emojis, looping videos, and an eraser to remove objects with background filling. In July 2017, users could add links to snaps, initially available only to brands, and new tools included "Backdrop" for cutting out and styling objects and "Voice Filters" for remixing voice sounds, with a dedicated speaker icon. In June 2020, Snap launched "minis," embeddable apps within the Snap app. In August 2022, "Family Center" was launched, allowing parents to monitor children aged 13–18. In September 2022, Snapchat for Web was introduced. In February 2023, "My AI" was launched for Snapchat+ users as a mobile version of ChatGPT, later made available to all users in April 2023, including for group chats. In June 2025, Snapchat released an app for the Apple Watch. Snaps can be personalized with visual effects, stickers, geofilters (available in specific locations, with a $10–15 fee per hour or annual plans from $1,000 to $10,000), and geostickers launched in 10 major cities in 2016. Bitmoji, personalized cartoon avatars, are used in snaps and messaging and can also serve as World Lenses. The "Lens" feature, introduced in September 2015, uses face detection to add real-time effects via long-pressing on a face. In April 2017, "World Lenses" were introduced, using augmented reality to place 3D elements into scenes. On October 26, 2018, Snapchat launched a desktop app for macOS and Windows, enabling lens use in video calls and live streaming on platforms like Skype, Twitch, YouTube, and Zoom, which was discontinued in January 2023. Snapchat also launched integration with Twitch, including in-stream widgets for Snapcodes, offering lenses to viewers and subscribers, and launched video game-themed lenses for League of Legends, Overwatch, and PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds. In August 2020, Snapchat collaborated with four TikTok influencers to launch AR lenses using geo-mapping and body tracking of 18 joints, generating effects around the user’s body. Brands like Coca-Cola, Pepsi, and Taco Bell now use AR lenses in advertising, making users part of the ad. In March 2022, users could share YouTube videos as stickers, functioning as clickable links. The "snapscore" tracks the number of snaps sent and received, visible to friends, showing a ratio of sent and received snaps. Synonyms include Snapchat points, Snapscore, Snap points, and Snap Number. For Snapchat Plus subscribers, best friends are represented as planets, expanding visual friendship displays beyond friend emojis. In October 2013, "My Story" was introduced, allowing users to compile snaps into chronological storylines accessible to friends. By June 2014, Stories surpassed private snaps as the most used feature, with over one billion views per day. In June 2014, the story feature expanded to include "Our Stories," later renamed to "Live Stories," allowing users at events to contribute to curated stories shared with all users, emphasizing public events over personal streams.

In October 2013, Snapchat introduced the "My Story" feature, enabling users to compile snaps into chronological storylines accessible to all their friends.[54][105] By June 2014, photo and video snaps in Stories had surpassed private person-to-person snaps as the most frequently used function, with over one billion views per day—double the daily views from April 2014.[106] The story feature was expanded in June 2014 to include "Our Stories," later renamed "Live Stories" a year later, allowing users at events like music festivals or sports events to contribute snaps to curated, publicly advertised stories from multiple perspectives. These stories could be localized, but Snapchat eventually scaled back personal imaging streams to emphasize public events.[107][108][109][110][111][112] In November 2015, an "Official Stories" designation was added to denote public stories by notable figures, similar to Twitter's "Verified account" program.[113] In January 2015, Snapchat launched "Discover," a section featuring ad-supported short-form content from major publishers such as BuzzFeed, CNN, ESPN, Mashable, People, Vice, and Snapchat itself.[114][115][116] To address data usage concerns, a "Travel Mode" option was introduced in August 2015, preventing automatic snap downloads until explicitly requested.[117] In October 2016, Snapchat replaced its auto-advance function with a "Story Playlist" feature, allowing users to select specific story thumbnails to play.[118][119] In January 2017, Snapchat revamped its design, adding search functionality and a new global live "Our Story" feature open to all users for contributions.[120] In May 2017, "Custom Stories" were introduced, enabling users to collaboratively create stories combining their captures.[121][122] In June 2017, "Snap Map" was launched, allowing users to optionally share their location with friends; a map accessible from the viewfinder lets users locate stories by location and use Bitmoji as place markers, with "Ghost Mode" hiding the user from the map. The feature is based on Zenly, acquired by Snap Inc. prior to launch, and uses data from OpenStreetMap and Mapbox, with satellite imagery from DigitalGlobe.[123][124][125][126] In February 2020, Snapchat released a Discover cartoon series called Bitmoji TV, starring users' avatars.[127] The Wall Street Journal reported in May 2017 that Snap Inc. had signed deals with NBCUniversal, A&E Networks, BBC, ABC, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, and others to develop original shows for Snapchat's Stories format, with each show lasting three to five minutes and detailed production reports sent to partners. Over 2017 and 2018, several shows were launched.[128][129][130] In 2018, Snapchat and Vertical Networks created "My Ex-BFF Court," a spoof of daytime TV court shows where ex-friends attempt to resolve conflicts, hosted by Judge Matteo Lane (Matthew Lane), with each episode featuring a funny sentence for the guilty party.[131] In 2018, Snapchat partnered with Fox to produce a television version of the dating and reality show "Phone Swap."[132] In 2018, Snapchat launched "How Low Will You Go," created by Above Average Productions and NBC.[133] Unlike other messaging apps, Evan Spiegel described Snapchat's messaging as "conversational" rather than "transactional," emphasizing real-time interactions similar to those with friends, contrasting with iMessage's interactions.[56] A blue pulsing "here" button appears in the sender's chat window when the recipient is viewing the chat, and holding it initiates a video chat. Messages disappear after being read, and a notification is sent only when the recipient starts typing. Users can reply to snaps within a story.[134] The video chat feature uses technology from AddLive, acquired by Snapchat prior to launch.[135] Spiegel argued that the "here" indicator is positive, signaling that a friend is present and fully engaged, unlike traditional online indicators that imply availability without intent to talk. The "Here" function avoids the awkwardness of typing indicators by maintaining fluid conversation flow.[56] On March 29, 2016, Snapchat launched "Chat 2.0," adding stickers, easier access to audio and video conferencing, the ability to leave audio or video "notes," and sharing recent camera photos, enabling seamless shifts between text, audio, and video chat.[136] In June 2018, Snapchat added the ability to delete a sent message (text, audio, or video) before it is read.[137][138] In August 2018, users could send Musical GIFs and TuneMojis.[139][140] In August 2022, Snap Inc. announced it would discontinue all original scripted content with no plans to continue in this area.[141] In 2023, Snapchat had over 300 million monthly active users.[7] In 2024, the countries with the most users were India (202.5 million), the United States (106.5 million), Pakistan (31.9 million), France (27.5 million), and the United Kingdom (23.1 million).[142] In January 2018, Snapchat introduced end-to-end encryption for snaps (photos and videos), according to a security engineer at the January 2019 Real World Crypto Conference; plans to extend encryption to text messages and group chats were announced at the same event.[143][144][145][146] Snapchat is popular among younger users, most between 18 and 24 in 2023, with an age rating of 12+ on the app store.[7][147] In 2014, researchers from the University of Washington and Seattle Pacific University conducted a survey on Snapchat use, originally hypothesizing that the ephemeral nature of messages would lead to privacy-sensitive content like sexting. However, only 1.6% of respondents reported using Snapchat primarily for sexting, while 14.2% admitted sending sexual content at some point.[148] The primary use was comedic content such as "stupid faces," reported by 59.8% of respondents.[148] Most users were unwilling to send content classified as sexting (74.8%), photos of documents (85.0%), messages with legally questionable content (86.6%), or mean or insulting content (93.7%).[148] The study found that Snapchat's success stems from its fun nature, not security, as 79.4% of users were aware that snaps could be recovered, and 52.8% reported this did not affect their behavior. Many users (52.8%) applied arbitrary timeout lengths to snaps regardless of content or recipient, while others adjusted timeouts based on trust, comprehension, or to avoid screenshots.[148] In the 2010s, Snapchat was seen as a messenger focused on in-the-moment sharing rather than permanent content accumulation.[149] As a mobile-first company, Snapchat did not need to transition to mobile like other social media networks, and Evan Spiegel described the app as primarily a camera company.[150][151] Spiegel dismissed comparisons to Facebook and Twitter, noting that major candidates occasionally used the app during the 2016 presidential race.[152] Snapchat offered distinct content through its Discover channel, separating brand and user-generated messaging.[153] Snapchat's features reflect a deliberate monetization strategy. On October 17, 2014, the company acknowledged its need for revenue and stated it wanted to deliver fun, informative ads, avoiding the creepiness of targeted ads. Its first paid ad, a 20-second trailer for the horror film Ouija, was shown on October 19, 2014.[154][155][156][157] In January 2015, Snapchat shifted from growth to monetization by launching "Discover," which allowed paid advertising from publishers, including CNN, Comedy Central, ESPN, and Food Network.[115][116][158] In June 2015, Snapchat allowed advertisers to purchase sponsored geofilters; McDonald's was an early customer, paying for a branded geofilter at its U.S. restaurant locations.[84] Snapchat promoted ad revenue from "Live Stories" in 2015, with ad placements or story sponsorships available, reaching an average of 20 million viewers in 24 hours.[110] In September 2015, Snapchat partnered with the National Football League to present live stories from selected games, including Sunday and marquee events like Monday Night Football and Thursday Night Football, with both parties contributing content and handling ad sales.[110][159] The 2015 Internet Trends Report by Mary Meeker noted that vertical video ads are watched in full nine times more than landscape ads.[160] In April 2016, NBC Olympics partnered with Snapchat to feature stories from the 2016 Summer Olympics in the U.S., including a behind-the-scenes Discover channel curated by BuzzFeed and stories combining NBC footage, athletes, and attendees. NBC sold ads and entered into revenue-sharing agreements, marking the first time Olympics content was featured on third-party property.[161] In May 2016, 20th Century Fox paid for all lenses to be tracking rolling out in June to select countries.[165][166] In 2017, Snapchat introduced "Snap to Store," allowing companies using geostickers to track whether users buy products or visit stores within seven days after seeing the sticker.[167][168] On November 13, 2018, Snapchat launched the Snap Store, selling Bitmoji merchandise personalized by user and friend avatars, including shirts, mugs, shower curtains, and phone cases.[169] In June 2018, Snapchat introduced Snap Kit, a third-party development platform with components including "Login Kit" (a social login platform using Snapchat accounts, offering privacy-conscious access with only display name and optional Bitmoji, subject to a 90-day inactivity timeout), "Creative Kit" (for apps to create stickers for Snapchat would diversify content by launching Snap Originals, including scripted shows and documentaries.[171][172][173] In June 2020, Snapchat launched its first "shoppable" original show, "The Drop," focusing on exclusive streetwear collages from celebrities and designers, with episodes explaining the item's creation and including a "swipe up to buy" action that updated the episode later that Snapchat made public the source code for an exploit on December 25, and on December 27 announced the implementation of mitigating features. However, an anonymous group hacked the platform, stating the features only presented "minor obstacles," and revealed approximately 4.6 million Snapchat usernames and phone numbers on a website called SnapchatDB.info, sending a statement to TechCrunch claiming their goal was to "raise public awareness... and... put public pressure on Snapchat" to fix the vulnerability. Snapchat apologized a week after the hack. In 2014, Snapchat settled a complaint by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), which alleged the company exaggerated how quickly messages would disappear; under the agreement, Snapchat agreed to have its privacy and security claims monitored by an independent party for 20 years and was prohibited from misrepresenting the extent to which it maintains user information confidentiality. Following this, Snapchat updated its privacy page to state it cannot guarantee messages will be deleted within a specific timeframe, noting that deleted data may remain in backups and that forensic tools can sometimes retrieve deleted data. In September 2024, the FTC released a report summarizing responses from nine companies—including Snapchat—to orders under Section 6(b) of the Federal Trade Commission Act of 1914, finding that companies' data practices exposed individuals to risks such as identity theft, stalking, emotional distress, mental health issues, social stigma, and reputational harm. In November 2014, Snapchat cracked down on third-party apps, removing 6snap and other apps from the Windows Phone Store in December, despite not developing an official app for the platform, which left users behind; a petition for an official app reached 43,000 signatures in 2015, but Snapchat did not respond or build an app, and later failed to develop one for Microsoft's Universal Windows Platform. In September 2015, an 18-year-old used Snapchat's "Lens" feature to record her driving speed at 107 mph (172 km/h) in Hampton, Georgia, leading to a crash that injured both drivers, with the Outlander driver requiring five weeks in intensive care and suffering a severe traumatic brain injury. In April 2016, the Outlander driver sued Snapchat and the user, alleging Snapchat knew the feature was being used for unlawful speed contests and failed to act. In October 2016, a similar crash occurred in Tampa, Florida, when a 22-year-old drove at 115 mph (185 km/h), killing five people. Former Snapchat employee Anthony Pompliano alleged in a 2015 lawsuit that co-founder Evan Spiegel stated Snapchat was "only for rich people" and that the company did not want to expand into poor countries like India and Spain, sparking a #UninstallSnapchat trend in India and resulting in a surge of one-star ratings on app stores, a 1.5% drop in Snapchat shares, and the company calling the claim "ridiculous" while asserting the app is available worldwide for free. In January 2017, Pompliano filed a lawsuit claiming Snapchat doctored growth metrics to deceive investors, asserting Spiegel dismissed his concerns and that he was fired afterward; the judge dismissed claims under the Dodd-Frank and Consumer Protection Acts due to an arbitration clause, but Snap Inc. faced backlash over lack of lawsuit disclosure, leading to falling stock prices, class-action lawsuits, and federal investigations. In June 2017, Snapchat launched "Snap Map," a feature that broadcasts user location on a map via opt-in, which reportedly does not fully explain the implications, such as continuous updates upon app opening and potential use by stalkers, and allows zooming to include street addresses; the Daily Telegraph reported police issued child safety warnings, and media raised safety concerns for teens and adults; Snapchat stated it prioritizes community safety and wants accurate information about how Snap Map works. Users can use "Ghost Mode" to select who sees their location, and Snapchat does not plan to run ads on Snap Map stories. Increased use of body and facial reshaping apps like Snapchat and Facetune has been linked to body dysmorphic disorder; in August 2018, Boston Medical Center researchers identified "Snapchat dysmorphia," where individuals seek surgery to match edited versions of themselves from Snapchat filters. In May 2019, multiple Snapchat employees used an internal tool called SnapLion—originally for law enforcement compliance—to spy on users. During the 2020 lockdown in France, Snapchat became a hub for distributing revenge porn of underage girls, with some perpetrators using explicit images to seek sexual favors or control. In 2020, a woman in North Carolina sued Snapchat, Tinder, and five men, claiming app features enabled her alleged rapist and friends to hide evidence of the rape, alleging Snapchat was specifically designed to serve as a secretive platform for non-consensual sexually explicit content and to operate as a safe haven from law enforcement. In December 2022, the National Crime Prevention Council urged U.S. Attorney General Merrick Garland to examine Snap's business practices related to selling fake pills containing lethal fentanyl; less than a month later, the FBI launched a probe into the company and the sale of fake pills. In November 2024, the NSPCC reported that Snapchat was the most popular app among online groomers, according to police statistics. In September 2015, Christal McGee drove her Mercedes-Benz C230 at 107 mph in Georgia and collided with a Mitsubishi Outlander, injuring the Outlander driver, Wentworth Maynard, who required five weeks of intensive care and suffered a permanent brain injury; in April 2016, Maynard sued McGee and Snapchat, claiming McGee used the "speed filter" at the time of the crash and that Snapchat negligently allowed the feature despite knowing it encouraged dangerous speeding. In March 2022, the Georgia Supreme Court ruled that Snapchat must face claims that it defectively designed the "speed filter." In May 2017, teens in Wisconsin used the "speed filter" to record a car reaching 123 mph on a rural road, leading to a crash that killed all three occupants; in May 2019, the families of passengers Hunter Morby and Landen Brown filed a lawsuit against Snapchat, alleging the company knew the filter encouraged reckless speeding but failed to restrict it; the case, Lemmon v. Snap, led to a landmark legal precedent when the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in May 2021 ruled that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act did not protect Snapchat from liability for negligent product design, distinguishing between liability for user-generated content and negligent design, allowing the case to proceed; in 2021, Snap Inc. settled the lawsuit for an undisclosed amount. In June 2021, Snapchat removed the "speed filter," citing limited use, following pressure from safety advocates, legal experts, and affected families who argued the filter incentivized reckless behavior among young drivers and called for greater accountability from social media companies. Snapchat's My Selfie feature allows users to use selfies with generative AI to create novel images, including a toggle to "See My Selfie in Ads" that is enabled by default. In September 2025, Snap Inc. announced it would charge users for storing more than five gigabytes of previously shared images and videos in Memories, a service previously offered with unlimited free storage, receiving widespread criticism as a "memory tax" and raising concerns about losing years of saved memories; the company claimed the change was for sustainability, but commentators described it as economic coercion based on cognitive vulnerabilities related to loss aversion. At the start of December 2025, Russia's internet and media regulator blocked Snapchat, citing use in "extremist and terrorist" activities, and on December 10, 2025, Australia banned Snapchat for users under 16 as part of the Online Safety Amendment.
